title: Rabbi Tzvi Frank
content:
Rabbi Tzvi Frank
This text is a comprehensive survey of the life and legacy of Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank, who was one of the most influential figures in shaping the religious establishment of Israel in the 20th century. The biographical essay traces his path from the Lithuanian yeshivot to the post of Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, emphasizing his unique ability to combine deep traditional learning with a statesmanlike vision of reviving Jewish sovereignty. The source examines in detail his key halakhic decisions at critical moments in history, such as the War of Independence, as well as his moderate approach to questions of agriculture and social cohesion. Ultimately, the text reveals the image of a leader who strove to turn the ancient laws of the Torah into a viable foundation for the life of a modern state, leaving behind a rich intellectual legacy and a dynasty integrated into all spheres of Israeli society.
The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of the Gaon Rabbi Tzvi Frank
The figure of the Gaon Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank (5633–5721; 1873–1960) stands as one of the most central and influential junctures in the shaping of renewed Jewish sovereignty and of the rabbinic establishment in the Land of Israel in the twentieth century.[1, 2, 3] He worked in a fateful period that stretched from the last years of Ottoman rule, through the days of the British Mandate, to the establishment of the State of Israel.[4] As the Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem and as a halakhic decisor of international stature, Rabbi Frank succeeded in combining deep, traditional Lithuanian erudition with a broad statesmanlike vision, moderate halakhic pluralism and deep concern for the needs of the individual and the community.[4, 5, 6] His Torah teaching and public work present a conception that identifies the Return to Zion as the beginning of the flowering of the redemption, and set out a halakhic teaching that translates the laws of the Torah into the conditions of modern life in a sovereign state.[2, 4, 7]
Biography and Formative Stations in His Life
Rabbi Frank's intellectual and spiritual roots are planted deep in the world of the Lithuanian yeshivot. He was born in the city of Kovno to his father, Rabbi Yehuda Leib Frank, who was one of the prominent leaders of the "Hibbat Zion" movement and was engaged in purchasing land in the Land of Israel.[1, 4, 8] In his youth he acquired Torah at the prestigious Telz yeshiva, where he enjoyed warm treatment and exceptional esteem from the head of the yeshiva, the Gaon Rabbi Eliezer Gordon, and later deepened his studies at the Slabodka yeshiva.[1, 8] In 5652 (1892) he immigrated to the Land together with his brother Tanchum, his sister Tzipporah and his cousin Rabbi Shmuel Hillel Shenkar, while his parents immigrated a year later and were central partners in founding the moshava of Hadera, where the father served as its first rabbi.[1, 8]
In Jerusalem Rabbi Frank continued his diligent Torah study at the "Etz Chaim" and "Torat Chaim" yeshivot.[2] In 5655 (1895) he married the granddaughter of Rabbi Chaim Yaakov Shapira, head of the rabbinic court of Rabbi Shmuel Salant, who had grown up in his home as his daughter.[2] This family tie brought him close to the supreme Torah leadership of Jerusalem.[2] Already when he was about 24, Rabbi Shmuel Salant recognized his exceptional genius and actively involved him in intricate deliberations on the laws of divorce, and even handed him the practical responsibility for halakhic rulings on the separation of terumot and ma'asrot (priestly and tithe portions).[3] In 5662 (1902) Rabbi Frank moved to study in Jaffa, and in Iyar 5664 (1904), when Rav Kook (the Raayah) arrived to serve as rabbi of Jaffa and the moshavot, deep bonds of friendship and mutual esteem were formed between the two that changed the face of religious history in the Land of Israel.[2] Encouraged by his wife's grandfather, Rabbi Shapira, he returned to Jerusalem and trained in practical halakhic ruling among the city's judges, until in 5667/5668 he was appointed an official judge in the rabbinic court of the Perushim at the Hurva of Rabbi Yehuda HeChasid.[1, 2, 9]
Public Leadership and the Founding of Torah Institutions in the Land of Israel
Rabbi Frank's public work was marked by the building of central leadership institutions and by the attempt to lead religious Judaism toward the challenges of sovereignty.[2, 7] The historic partnership with Rav Kook gave rise to the initiative to establish a joint "Committee of Rabbis" for Ashkenazim and Sephardim in Jerusalem, a preparatory step that formed the basis for the establishment of the Chief Rabbinate of Israel in 5681 (1921).[2] Rabbi Frank worked tirelessly for the election of Rav Kook as rabbi of Jerusalem and afterwards as the first Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi, while he himself served as a member of the Council of the Chief Rabbinate and as head of the Great Rabbinical Court for about four decades.[2, 9] On 1 Tevet 5696 (1936), a few months after the passing of Rav Kook, Rabbi Frank was elected unanimously as the Ashkenazi rabbi of Jerusalem, receiving the signatures of all the city's rabbis from various circles, and bearing overall responsibility for the systems of kashrut, the eruv, the mikvaot and ritual slaughter.[2, 7]
Rabbi Frank's approach to public leadership went beyond the rigid conservatism of the Old Yishuv.[4] He distinctly opposed the position led by Rabbi Diskin, and sought to establish a rabbinic path that would form a living and courageous bridge between the world of Torah and the agricultural, laboring settlement.[4] This insight explains his joining the "Bnei Torah" association, which sought to combine a life of Torah thought with the establishment of independent agricultural settlement, as well as his educational work at the "Sha'arei Torah" Talmud Torah in Jaffa, which was meant to train spiritual leaders with a practical understanding of the realities of the Land of Israel.[4]
On the other hand, Rabbi Frank's last years were marked by a conscious and disappointed distancing from the institutions he had helped to establish.[1] For the six years preceding his death, the rabbi refrained from taking part in the sessions of the Council of the Chief Rabbinate, and even sent an open letter of support for the boycott that rabbis had imposed on the elections to the Chief Rabbinate.[1] This sharp position stemmed from his fear of the loss of the institution's spiritual independence and its subjection to political and party struggles, a step that highlights his intellectual integrity and his refusal to sacrifice the honor of the Torah for the sake of institutional interests.[1]
Ruling in a Time of National Emergency and the War of Independence
During the War of Independence and the heavy siege of Jerusalem in 5708, Rabbi Frank ruled out of a deep commitment to collective life-saving.[3] He permitted the manufacture of armored vehicles on the Sabbath for the rescue and defense of Gush Etzion, while stressing meticulously that this permission applied solely to actions necessary for saving life, and forbade any desecration of the Sabbath that was not directly essential to the war effort.[3] Because of the hunger and the severe shortage of food in the besieged city, he ruled courageously that the Ashkenazi public was permitted to consume kitniyot (legumes) and legume by-products (legume oil) on the festival of Passover of 5708.[1, 3] After the fall of the Jewish Quarter in the Old City, he set the 20th of Sivan 5708 as a communal day of mourning and prayer marking thirty days since the destruction of the Quarter and its fall.[3] Alongside these permissions, he showed firm opposition to the conscription of yeshiva students into the army, out of a deep belief that Torah study serves as a spiritual protective wall that shields the fighters at the front.[3]
His halakhic and social sensitivity stood out especially in his determined struggle against autopsies not required for urgent medical need, a struggle that led him to oppose the Anatomy and Pathology Law and even to permit yeshiva students to secretly smuggle the bodies of the deceased out of hospitals in order to prevent their dissection.[3] Nevertheless, displaying a balanced and uncompromising capacity for ruling, he permitted an autopsy on the body of a person killed in a road accident in a case where the autopsy was the only means of proving the guilt of a negligent driver in court.[3] This decision stemmed from the principle of "migdar milta" (making a fence for the matter): the burning social need to prevent killers on the roads from evading punishment and to protect public safety, which demonstrates his readiness to prefer the repair of society in extreme situations over common halakhic prohibitions.[3]
The Commandments Dependent on the Land and the Shemitah Controversy
Rabbi Frank's rulings on the agunot of the Holocaust and of Israel's wars won him lasting renown as a judge of deep compassion and public courage.[3] When he came to write complex rulings that released women from their status as agunot, he adopted a unique and deliberate strategy: he systematically refrained from detailing the reasons, sources and halakhic dialectics that underlay the permission.[2] This insight stemmed from his understanding of scholarly dynamics; he feared that rabbis or Torah scholars in later generations would try to find refutations or difficulties in his proofs, which would cast doubt on the validity of the second marriages and could lead to a fear of mamzerut (illegitimacy) among the seed of Israel.[2] By omitting the reasons, Rabbi Frank established a fait accompli according to which his public and spiritual authority as rabbi of Jerusalem was entirely sufficient, and thereby blocked in advance any opening for appeals at the expense of the women who had been released.[2]
On the question of Shemitah (the sabbatical year) and the commandments dependent on the Land, Rabbi Frank's teaching stood in marked contrast to the insular and stringent approach of the author of "Chazon Ish."[2, 4] Whereas the Chazon Ish addressed an elite group of farmers who kept Shemitah without compromise, Rabbi Frank saw his role as a religious leader of the whole community.[4] He firmly defended the "heter mechira" (sale permit) instituted by Rav Kook, seeing it as a vital tool and a necessary emergency measure to prevent the economic collapse of the Hebrew agricultural settlement.[2, 4] For those who wished to be stringent and not rely on the permit, he proposed an alternative practical solution: consuming vegetables and fruit grown in the Jordan Valley region (such as in the kibbutzim Degania and Afikim), since this region is considered outside the borders of those who came up from Babylon, and therefore the obligation of the seventh year there is lighter, being rabbinic.[2]
The deepening of the foundations of the "heter mechira" found brilliant expression in his rulings in the collection Har Tzvi, Zera'im (Part 2, siman 47).[10] Relying on the ruling of the "Torat Chesed," Rabbi Frank determined that it is permitted to exchange land or a house in the Land of Israel with a gentile, and that this does not violate the prohibition of "lo techonem" (you shall not give them a foothold in the land).[10] He explained that the Torah prohibition was meant to prevent the influence of idolatry and intermarriage, and therefore does not apply when the sale is made to a ger toshav (a resident alien who keeps the seven Noahide commandments) or when the purpose of the transaction is the personal benefit of the Jew and the economic strengthening of the settlement in the Land.[10, 11] Although Maimonides (Rambam) ruled that at a time when the Jubilee is not in force a ger toshav is not accepted, Rabbi Frank held that the very observance of these principles among the gentiles in the Land removes the essential concern of "lo techonem" and allows the sale to be carried out for the sake of saving Hebrew agriculture.[10, 11]
His Torah Teaching and Writings
Rabbi Frank's approach to study combined Lithuanian pilpul and analysis with the striving for decided, practical halakha in the manner of Rabbi Shmuel Salant.[3, 8] A clear example of his scientific and precise thinking is his ruling on an electric Hanukkah menorah.[1] Rabbi Frank ruled that one does not fulfill the obligation by lighting an electric lamp fed from the general power grid (one not based on batteries).[1] His halakhic reasoning was based on the fact that halakha requires that at the time of the act of lighting, the full measure of fuel needed for burning for at least half an hour after the appearance of the stars be present in the lamp.[1] Since in an electric lamp connected to the grid the current of electrons is generated and flows dynamically, renewed at every single moment from the power station, the lamp cannot be regarded as containing all the "fuel" at the moment of lighting, and therefore the act lacks the halakhic definition of "lighting" in a vessel.[1]
Family Lineage and Influence for Generations
One of the unique features of Rabbi Frank's legacy is the fascinating integration of his descendants into all strata of Israeli and Jewish society: from the world of Torah and the yeshivot, through the world of education and society, to the modern political and technological system.[1]
Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank passed away on 21 Kislev 5721 (10 December 1960) at the age of 87 and was buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.[1, 3] His death aroused profound national mourning; many thousands accompanied him on his final journey, the rabbinical courts throughout the country closed as a sign of mourning, and the cabinet meeting was postponed to allow the ministers to take part in his state funeral.[1] His halakhic legacy remains engraved as a model of leadership of great stature, combining absolute commitment to halakha with a statesmanlike vision that understands the needs of the hour of the people of Israel in its Land.[4, 5]

title: Halakhic Leadership in an Era of Revival and Rebirth: The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank
source_file: מנהיגות הלכתית בעידן של תחייה ותקומה- פועלו ומשנתו התורנית של הרב צבי פסח פראנק.docx
content:
Halakhic Leadership in an Era of Revival and Rebirth: The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank
His Life: From the Lithuanian Beit Midrash to the Heart of Jerusalem Activity
Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank (5633–5721, 1873–1960) stands as one of the central figures in the world of halakha and rabbinic leadership in the twentieth century [cite: 1, 2]. His halakhic teaching and public activity form an essential connecting link between the learning tradition of the Lithuanian yeshivot and the national, social and technological challenges that arose with the revival of the Hebrew Yishuv and the establishment of the State of Israel [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4].
Rabbi Frank was born in the city of Kovno in Lithuania in 5633 (1873), to his mother Malka and his father Rabbi Yehuda Leib Frank, who was one of the leaders of the local "Hovevei Zion" movement [cite: 1, 2]. He acquired his early Torah education at the Telz yeshiva, where he enjoyed special treatment and particular closeness from the head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Eliezer Gordon, and later he studied Torah at the Slobodka yeshiva [cite: 1, 2]. This learning environment gave him a sharp and profound method of analysis, which served as a firm foundation for the swift and well-grounded capacity for halakhic ruling that he displayed throughout his life [cite: 1, 2, 5].
In 5653 (1893) Rabbi Frank immigrated to the Land of Israel, slightly preceding his parents, who were among the founders of the moshava of Hadera, where his father even served as its first rabbi [cite: 1, 2]. The deep attachment to settling the Land was a fundamental component of the family identity, but it was also accompanied by a heavy personal price in blood, when his sister Yenta Tzipora and her husband Rabbi Avraham Yaakov Orlansky (the rabbi of Zikhron Yaakov) were murdered together with members of their family in the riots of 5689 in Hebron [cite: 2].
Upon his arrival in Jerusalem, Rabbi Frank joined the study at the "Torat Chaim" and "Etz Chaim" yeshivot [cite: 1, 2]. During this period his figure caught the eye of the leader of the Ashkenazi community in Jerusalem, Rabbi Shmuel Salant, who recognized his leadership potential and paired him as a study partner (chavruta) with Rabbi Yechiel Michel Tucazinsky [cite: 2]. In 5655 (1895) he married Gita Malka, the daughter of Rabbi David Shapira and granddaughter of the head of the rabbinic court (Ravad) of the Edah HaChareidit, Rabbi Chaim Yaakov Shapira, a marriage that brought him even closer to the core of the spiritual leadership of the Old City and made him the brother-in-law of Rabbi Aryeh Levin [cite: 1, 2].
In his first years in Jerusalem he lived in the Strauss courtyard, was among those who attended the Saturday-night lessons of Rabbi Yehoshua Leib Diskin, and in 5657 (1897) he joined the "Beit HaMussar" founded under the inspiration of the Alter of Kelm [cite: 2]. Between 5662 and 5664 (1902–1904) he moved to Jaffa and served as a teacher (ram) in the yeshiva attached to the "Sha'arei Torah" Talmud Torah, a period in which deep creative ties and friendship were kindled between him and the rabbi of the city at the time, Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook [cite: 2]. Upon his return to Jerusalem he began teaching at the Etz Chaim, Sha'ar HaShamayim and Torat Emet yeshivot, and received ordination (semikha) as an official halakhic decisor (moreh hora'ah) from Rabbi Salant and from Rabbi Chaim Yaakov Shapira [cite: 2].
Leadership of the Rabbinic Court and the Rabbinate of the City of Jerusalem
Rabbi Frank's legal and public standing took shape through his institutional judicial work. In 5667 (1907) he was appointed an associate judge (dayan) in the Ashkenazi-Perushi rabbinic court in Jerusalem headed by Rabbi Yaakov Leib Levi, and a year later he was appointed a permanent member of the court alongside Rabbi Moshe Nachum Wallenstein and Rabbi Aryeh Leib Hershler [cite: 2]. At the end of the First World War, in 5678 (1918), he rose to serve as head of the rabbinic court (av beit din), a position he held for forty consecutive years [cite: 2]. His judicial outlook consistently preferred the path of compromise and agreed settlement over a rigid decision according to Torah law, out of the view that the role of the court is not limited merely to issuing a verdict but serves as an instrument for establishing social peace [cite: 2].
He served as a key figure in the establishment of the Chief Rabbinate of Israel in 5681 (1921), and was among the initiators of bringing Rav Kook (the Ra'ayah) to serve as the rabbi of Jerusalem and afterwards as Chief Rabbi [cite: 1, 2, 4, 6]. Within this framework he served as head (Ravad) of the Great Rabbinic Court and as a member of the Council of the Chief Rabbinate [cite: 1, 2]. After the passing of Rav Kook in 5696 (1936), Rabbi Frank was chosen to serve as the Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, a tenure that lasted until his death on 20 Kislev 5721 (1960) [cite: 1, 4].
His public leadership faced a supreme test during the War of Independence and the siege of Jerusalem in 5708 (1948). At a time when an existential threat hung over the community, Rabbi Frank exercised his halakhic authority to permit emergency activities on the Sabbath, such as the manufacture and reinforcement of armored vehicles for the fighters in Gush Etzion, while drawing a careful distinction between needs that are clearly a matter of saving life (pikuach nefesh) and desecration of the Sabbath that is not necessary [cite: 2]. Because of the severe shortage of food in the besieged city, he permitted, in an unprecedented manner, the eating of legumes (kitniyot) on Passover 5708 for all residents of Jerusalem [cite: 2]. On the other hand, he maintained a firm position regarding the status of yeshiva students and opposed their conscription, out of a faith-based view that toil in Torah constitutes a vital protective component of the nation's security [cite: 2]. With the fall of the Old City, he declared 20 Sivan 5708 a day of mourning and prayer marking thirty days since its loss [cite: 2].
Role and institution | Period of tenure | Main activities and systemic influence
Dayan and head of the rabbinic court in Jerusalem | 5668–5718 (1908–1958) [cite: 2] | Consolidation of the Ashkenazi judicial system, a policy of preferring compromise, and the release of agunot [cite: 2, 7].
One of the founders of the Chief Rabbinate of Israel | 5681 (1921) onward [cite: 1, 2, 4] | Shaping the institutional structure of the state rabbinate, serving as head of the Great Rabbinic Court [cite: 1, 2].
Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem | 5696–5721 (1936–1960) [cite: 1, 4] | Leading the city during the periods of the riots, the siege in the War of Independence and the establishment of the State [cite: 2, 4].
Head of the "Midrash Bnei Zion" yeshiva | The 1930s to the 1950s [cite: 1] | Training Torah scholars to specialize in the commandments dependent on the Land and in practical halakhic ruling [cite: 1, 3].
His Torah Writings and the Methodology of His Rulings
Rabbi Frank's method of ruling is distinguished by purposefulness, clarity and a striving for a clear practical decision. Unlike authors who expanded at length in hypothetical analytical pilpul, his responsa present a concentrated analysis of the Talmudic passages and of the halakhic decisors, leading directly to the bottom line of practical halakha [cite: 5]. This approach made his books fundamental works for dayanim and halakhic decisors.
His central work, the responsa "Har Tzvi", covered the four parts of the Shulchan Arukh – Orach Chaim, Yoreh De'ah, Even HaEzer and Choshen Mishpat [cite: 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. The name of the book is derived from his name (his surname "Frank" alongside his first name Tzvi) [cite: 8, 11, 12]. This series contains hundreds of responsa sent to him from all over the Land and the Diaspora, and it reflects his engagement with the gravest questions of the hour facing the public and the individual [cite: 2, 5].
Another series of works of wide influence is "Mikra'ei Kodesh", which focuses on comprehensive halakhic monographs on the laws of the holidays, the festivals and the seasons of the year [cite: 8, 9, 10]. In these books Rabbi Frank examines the foundations of the commandments of each holiday, while incorporating the customs of Jerusalem and the rulings of the sages of his generation [cite: 8, 9, 10]. Alongside these, he published numerous pamphlets on ritual slaughter, terumot and ma'asrot (tithes) and the laws of the sanctity of the Land, beginning in 5668 (1908), which shaped the norms of medicine, agriculture and religion in the young state [cite: 2, 3, 13].
Fundamental Issues in His Halakhic Teaching
Sabbath, Electricity and Modern Industry
Rabbi Frank was among the first halakhic decisors to delve deeply into the halakhic significance of the use of electrical energy on the Sabbath [cite: 11, 12]. His analyses were based on a sharp physical understanding of electrical systems, while defining distinct boundaries between Torah (de'oraita) prohibitions and rabbinic (de-rabbanan) ones [cite: 11, 12].
On the question of using electric current produced in power stations by Jewish workers on the Sabbath, Rabbi Frank sought ways of leniency for the general public in the responsa "Har Tzvi" (Orach Chaim, siman 180) [cite: 11]. He relied on halakhic principles such as "commandments were not given for enjoyment" with regard to Torah study and religious needs, and on the absence of direct intent on the part of the electric company workers for any specific person [cite: 11]. Nevertheless, he supported and recommended connecting to a private generator as a means of enhanced observance (hiddur) and of avoiding benefit from public desecration of the Sabbath [cite: 11].
Another central issue was discussed in the responsa "Har Tzvi" (Orach Chaim, siman 181) concerning opening the door of an electric refrigerator on the Sabbath [cite: 11]. Rabbi Frank established a halakhic principle according to which opening the door is not considered a direct activation of the motor but an act of "preserving the existing state", whose purpose is to prevent the spoilage of food, and he therefore ruled to permit its use [cite: 11]. In his discussions of changing the intensity of the current in closed electrical circuits (Orach Chaim, siman 173), he drew a conceptual distinction between creating a new circuit (molid or boneh) and changing the intensity of the current in an existing circuit, a distinction that served as the basis for later discussions on public and medical equipment [cite: 12].
The Land of Israel, Agriculture and the State
Rabbi Frank's rulings on the commandments dependent on the Land were marked by support for settlement and for securing the economic existence of the Hebrew economy [cite: 2, 3, 13]. He continued the policy of Rabbi Shmuel Salant and supported the implementation of the "heter mechira" (sale permit) in the Sabbatical year (shemitah) as a necessary emergency measure to prevent the collapse of agriculture [cite: 2, 3, 13]. He insisted that the sale be carried out with strict legal precision, while preserving the connection to the Land [cite: 3, 13].
On the issue of new agricultural technologies, such as water-based cultivation (hydroponics), he ruled that plants growing on a water medium are considered field crops in every respect, and therefore the laws of terumot and ma'asrot apply to them [cite: 13]. After the War of Liberation, he became involved in a complex halakhic-political dispute with the Rishon LeZion, Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Chai Uziel, concerning the legal and halakhic status of fruit and orchards in the territories conquered by the IDF [cite: 3]. This discussion revolved around the interpretation of the law of "conquest in war" and its effect on the obligation to separate terumot and ma'asrot, while defining the civil and state ownership of this fruit [cite: 3].
The Release of Agunot
Rabbi Frank's work in the field of releasing agunot is considered one of the most remarkable and sensitive chapters of his leadership [cite: 2, 7]. Following the destruction of European Jewry in the Holocaust and complex combat events in the War of Independence, thousands of intricate cases of agunot reached his door [cite: 2, 7].
In this work he combined halakhic creativity, courage and deep human sensitivity [cite: 7]. His methodology was unique: when he brought additional rabbis to join in a permission, he deliberately refrained from asking and knowing their exact reasons, so as not to come to a discussion that might contradict their proofs and thereby annul the permission [cite: 2]. On the other hand, he came out firmly against proposals for the collective release of agunot, and insisted that each and every case be examined individually and meticulously [cite: 2]. In addition, he worked for the appointment of a dedicated rabbi to the Hadassah Medical Center in order to ensure the proper arrangement of divorces (gittin) for terminally ill patients, with the aim of preventing situations of agunah status and complex levirate release (chalitza) [cite: 2].
His Students, His Influence and His Legacy
Rabbi Frank served as a living bridge between the world of the old Jerusalem and the institutions of the new state [cite: 2, 4]. His moderate positions, his love for every Jew and his Torah integrity positioned him as a figure accepted by all circles – from the Edah HaChareidit, through religious Zionism, to the secular leadership of the Yishuv [cite: 4]. He showed a firm stance against extremist elements in Jerusalem and in Bnei Brak, while preserving the independence of his rulings [cite: 4].
Among his students and those directly influenced by him are the great halakhic decisors of the next generation:
Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv: served alongside him in the rabbinic court in Jerusalem, and adopted his factual and focused approach to analysis in matters of agunot and marriage.
Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach: maintained close scholarly ties with him, especially on matters of technology, electricity and medicine on the Sabbath, and continued the path of realistic halakhic ruling [cite: 11].
Rabbi Aryeh Levin: his brother-in-law and close partner in Torah enterprises, acts of kindness and visits to prisoners [cite: 2].
Rabbi Yitzchak Arieli: one of the heads of the Mercaz HaRav yeshiva, who was a partner in his central halakhic discussions.
Rabbi Frank's institutional and halakhic contribution continues to resonate in the working structure of the rabbinic courts in Israel, in the public kashrut system and in modern mechanisms of halakhic ruling [cite: 2, 3, 4]. His legacy presents a model of a halakhic decisor who combines profound scholarship, national responsibility and human kindness [cite: 2, 3, 7].
Summary
The work and Torah teaching of Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank constitute an enduring asset in the development of halakha in the generation of national rebirth [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4]. From his formative years in the Lithuanian beit midrash in Kovno, through his long tenure as head of the rabbinic court and Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, to his Torah works "Responsa Har Tzvi" and "Mikra'ei Kodesh", Rabbi Frank led a courageous, measured and purposeful line of halakhic ruling [cite: 1, 2, 5, 7, 8]. His pioneering rulings on matters of electricity, agriculture, war and the release of agunot established his standing as the halakhic decisor of the generation, who succeeded in steering the ship of halakha through the dramatic transformations of the twentieth century with absolute fidelity to tradition and responsibility for the whole of Israel [cite: 2, 3, 7, 11, 13].
